abstract: Genetic diversity is a fundamental component of biodiversity, and temporal genomics offers a powerful approach to monitoring genomic erosion and informing conservation assessments. However, robust inference of genetic diversity loss requires consistency with demographic expectations and careful evaluation of technical biases between historical and modern sequencing data. Here, we combine population-genetic simulations, independent reanalyses of temporal genomic datasets, comparisons of alternative heterozygosity estimators and controlled experiments of historical-like DNA degradation to evaluate the reliability of genomic erosion estimates. Using data from four bird species included in a recent study reporting average diversity losses of 43-49% across 62 species (Liu et al., 2026), we show that losses of this magnitude generally require severe, sustained population bottlenecks accompanied by extensive runs of homozygosity (ROH), which were uncommon in the modern genomes examined. Heterozygosity estimates were highly sensitive to analytical methods: ANGSD recovered substantial declines (23-42%), whereas HEARTY and ATLAS showed little or no loss (-1% to +9%). Experimentally introducing historical-like DNA degradation into reads from genetically identical individuals generated apparent declines of up to 42% with ANGSD, demonstrating that sequencing artefacts alone can produce signals comparable to those reported. We further evaluated estimator performance using the Chatham Island black robin, which experienced a documented severe demographic collapse. HEARTY and ATLAS recovered substantial heterozygosity losses (56-59%), although additional degradation experiments revealed dataset-specific biases in both methods. Together, our findings demonstrate that technical artefacts can mimic or obscure genuine genomic erosion, with effects varying across datasets and analytical approaches. Integrating demographic expectations, complementary genomic indicators and explicit assessments of sequencing biases is essential for reliable use of temporal genomics in biodiversity monitoring and conservation assessments.
